description: Lunar Navigator compares sunlight and Earth visibility at lunar landing sites using measured NASA terrain. It adapts the Ohio Lunar Planner method into a browser workspace with scenario comparisons, timelines, saved inputs and reproducible exports.
summary: Lunar Navigator helps you compare places to land near the Moon’s south pole. Pick a location and a date to see when the Sun and Earth are visible. The app uses NASA terrain data and calculations from Ohio University’s Lunar Planner. You can compare two sites, play the timeline, and look at the Sun and Earth above the nearby hills. You can also save your setup or download the results. This helps explain why a site with more sunlight might have less time with Earth in view. The estimates are for learning and early planning.
details:
The app compares lunar landing sites and dates. You can pick a listed site or enter coordinates. Change the arrival date or the height above the ground, then compare the results.

The timeline shows how the Sun and Earth move above the local terrain. The results show how long the Sun or Earth stays out of view. You can save your setup to open it later, or download the results as JSON or CSV files.

The calculations come from Ohio University’s Lunar Planner. NASA terrain measurements show which hills block the view. The app checks the Sun and Earth every 15 minutes.

The app is written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A browser worker runs the calculations so the controls can stay usable. The layout uses the open-source Tabler template. The terrain files are included with the app, and no account is needed to use it.

The model has limits. Small ridges can disappear in the reduced terrain data. The Sun and Earth positions are approximate, and events can happen between the 15-minute checks. Seeing Earth does not prove a radio link will work. Sunlight visibility does not tell you how much electricity a solar panel will make. The app is for learning and early site comparisons, not flight or landing-safety decisions.

We used OpenAI Codex to help with research, code, debugging, writing, layout and demo editing. The video shows the real app. It includes a label explaining the AI help. The NASA data and Ohio Lunar Planner method were reused. We did not train a new model, and the app does not run an AI model.

Code, tests and credits: https://github.com/danielli223/lunar-navigator
